questions.question: Describe desert and semi-desert climates and explain why many hot deserts form where they do.
questions.expected_answer: Desert: less than about 250 mm of rain a year, very unreliable, with evaporation far greater than precipitation; hot inland deserts have summer days above 45 °C and a daily range over 20 °C because clear, dry air lets heat escape at night; coastal deserts beside cold currents are cooler and foggy. Semi-desert or steppe: about 250 to 500 mm, unreliable with frequent droughts, low shrubs, grasses and succulents, as in the Karoo, Northern Cape and Sahel; Upington gets about 190 mm with 35 °C summer days and frosty winter nights. Causes: hot deserts lie at about 15 to 35 degrees in subtropical high-pressure belts where air sinks, warms and dries; many lie on western coasts beside cold currents that stabilise the air, such as the Namib beside the Benguela and the Atacama beside the Humboldt.

questions.question: Compare the Mediterranean climate of Cape Town with the continental climate of Moscow.
questions.expected_answer: Cape Town, Mediterranean, on the western side of the continent at about 34 degrees south: January about 21 °C, July about 12 to 13 °C, range about 9 °C; about 500 mm mostly from May to August; dry, sunny summers under subtropical high pressure and wet winters when westerlies and cold fronts arrive; fynbos, vineyards, wheat, deciduous fruit. Moscow, continental, deep inside a large northern continent at about 56 degrees north: January about −6 °C, July about 19 °C, range about 25 °C; about 700 mm with a summer maximum and winter snow; far from the sea, so large ranges with long cold winters; grassland and taiga. Cape Town's maritime position and lower latitude keep it mild; Moscow's inland position and higher latitude bring extremes.

questions.question: Describe polar, tundra and high mountain climates, giving an example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Polar ice cap: high latitudes such as Antarctica and Greenland; no month above 0 °C; very low snowfall, often under 100 mm in the interior, making it a cold desert; record about −89 °C at Vostok in 1983. Tundra: around the Arctic Ocean in northern Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Siberia; warmest month between 0 and 10 °C, long very cold winters, low precipitation, permafrost with a thawing boggy top layer in summer; mosses, lichens, grasses and low shrubs, no trees; caribou and Arctic foxes; Inuit and Sámi peoples. High mountain: the Andes, Himalayas, Ethiopian Highlands, Lesotho highlands; temperature falls with height, giving stacked zones of climate and vegetation, intense sunshine, rapid weather changes and cold nights; Andean crops vary with height and Lesotho's highlands get winter snow.
